title_zh: Randy Cohen：液态私募股权（Liquid PE）如何把 60/40 组合升级为 50/30/20
subtitle_zh: 哈佛商学院教授 Randy Cohen 谈用因子与对冲在公开市场复制私募股权业绩。
summary_zh: 本期 Alpha Exchange 中，主持人 Dean Curnutt 对话 Harvard Business School 金融与创业学教授、PEO Partners 联合创始人 Randy Cohen——两人同为 1990 年代芝加哥大学博士项目出身、都师从 Gene Fama。Cohen 回顾学术路径：早期做 Fama-French 式实证，后在博士论文里为“市场崩盘时预期收益偏高”这一谜题寻找风险与行为之外的“第三条路”——机构投资者的代理问题（agency problem），即他们为避免在下跌时被解雇而减仓、在高位补回。本集核心是“液态私募股权”（liquid PE）：用因子与对冲在公开市场复制私募股权业绩。他指出传统 PE 每年收费常超 700 个基点，而液态 PE 的 ETF 或共同基金仅约 100 个基点，600bp 的鸿沟意味着即便毛收益落后 3%-6%，净收益（net basis）仍能与 PE 打平甚至领先。他还提出“LBO 目标公司”的五个特征——高盈利、高派息、低倍数、低风险、小规模——恰恰对应 Fama-French 五因子。液态 PE 未必与传统 PE 竞争，而是帮投不起百万门槛的人把组合从 60/40 升级到 50/30/20，也为机构投资者充当流动性缓冲与完成性组合（completion portfolios）。节目尾声谈到生成式 AI（如 Claude）如何颠覆实证金融研究：过去需数千小时研究助理的工作如今可由 AI 完成，让人能从 50 个点子里筛出真正管用的 6 个再逐一核查。是一集关于因子、PE 复制与研究范式变革的深谈。

turns.en: That's why I think the idea of liquid PE is so powerful and you notice it doesn't have to compete with the, the notion is not, oh my gosh, people should ditch their PE and put it in liquid PE.
turns.zh: 这就是为什么我觉得“液态私募股权”（liquid PE）这个理念如此强大——你注意到，它并不一定要跟传统私募股权去竞争，它的想法不是“天哪，大家应该把私募股权都撤掉，改投液态私募股权”。

turns.en: The idea is for investors who can't invest in private equity because they're just not rich enough to make million dollar minimums. This is a solution to take their portfolio from 6040 to 5030-20 and for institutional investors and wealthy families who are PE investors, this can play a really useful role as a tool in the toolbox for them as a liquidity buffer for completion portfolios, for other kinds of applications that are hard to do with traditional PE.
turns.zh: 它的定位是：对于那些投不起私募股权的人——他们还没富有到能满足一百万美元起投门槛——这是一个解决方案，可以把他们的组合从 60/40 调整到 50/30/20；而对于那些本身就是私募股权投资者的机构投资者和富裕家族，它作为工具箱里的一个工具也能发挥非常实用的作用——充当流动性缓冲、用于完成性组合（completion portfolios），以及很多传统私募股权难以实现的其他用途。

turns.en: Hello, this is Dean Kernott and welcome to the Alpha Exchange, where we explore topics in financial markets associated with managing risk, generating return, and the deployment of capital in the alternative investment industry.
turns.zh: 你好，我是 Dean Kernott，欢迎收听 Alpha Exchange。在这个节目里，我们探讨金融市场中与风险管理、收益创造以及另类投资行业中资本配置相关的话题。

turns.en: I'm joined today by Randy Cohen. He is a professor of finance and entrepreneurship at Harvard Business School, also a co-founder of PEO Partners.
turns.zh: 今天和我一起的是 Randy Cohen。他是哈佛商学院（Harvard Business School）的金融与创业学教授，也是 PEO Partners 的联合创始人。

turns.en: Randy, it has been great to reconnect with you recently and it's a pleasure to welcome you to the podcast. Thanks so much for having me, Dean.
turns.zh: Randy，最近能跟你重新联系上真的很高兴，也非常欢迎你来到我们的播客。——谢谢你邀请我，Dean。

turns.en: Obviously, you and I met all the way back in PhD program at Chicago in the 90s when I was studying there and we started arguing about philosophy and politics and finance and everything from the very beginning and it has been great to reconnect in recent years and get to renew the conversation.
turns.zh: 显然，你我和我早在上世纪 90 年代的芝加哥博士项目里就认识了，那时我在那里读书，我们从一开始就在争论哲学、政治、金融以及各种话题，所以这些年能重新联系上、把这段对话续上，感觉特别好。

turns.en: I was a 24-year-old at the University of Chicago. I was one of the brave ones that took Pharma's class. I was writing in the, forget what it was called, the GSB newspaper.
turns.zh: 我在芝加哥大学那会儿才 24 岁。我是那些胆子够大、去选了 Fama 那门课的人之一。我当时还在——忘了那报纸叫什么了——GSB 校报上写东西。

turns.en: You and I went back and forth and then I learned that you were the TA for the Pharma class. That was a lot of fun. If you have those articles, scan them and send them to me because I love seeing, I had a funny experience recently.
turns.zh: 你我和我在那报纸上来来往往地争论，后来我才知道你原来是 Fama 那门课的助教（TA）。那段经历特别有意思。你要是还留着那些文章，扫描一下发给我，我特别喜欢看——我最近还有件挺逗的事。

turns.en: I got a text from my brother. He was going through old junk in his basement and he came upon a copy of our high school newspaper and he's like, why do I still have this?
turns.zh: 我收到我哥发来的短信。他在地下室翻旧杂物，结果翻出一份我们的中学报纸，他就纳闷：我怎么还留着这玩意儿？

turns.en: And then he looked and it was because it was an op-ed by me and he scanned it and texted it to me and I read that I wrote it when I was 15 years old and I was like, oh my God, it sounds exactly like me.
turns.zh: 然后他一看，那上面有一篇是我写的评论版文章（op-ed），他就扫描下来发给我，我读到我写它的时候才 15 岁，我当时就想，天哪，听起来完全就是现在的我。

turns.en: I was the exact same guy when I was 15 and that was fun to see. Consistent. I like it. So, you have a PhD from the University of Chicago. You've spent your career in academic research, in teaching.
turns.zh: 我 15 岁的时候和现在这个人一模一样，看到这些挺有意思的。——真够始终如一的，我喜欢。那么，你拥有芝加哥大学的博士学位，你的整个职业生涯都投入在学术研究和教学上。

turns.en: You've done a lot of different research in the realm of empirical finance. Why don't you just take us a little bit through your journey, maybe starting with the University of Chicago and then into the founding, which is going to be a part of our conversation of PEO partners.
turns.zh: 你在实证金融这个领域做了大量不同的研究。不如你带我们简单回顾一下你的旅程，也许就从芝加哥大学开始，然后讲到那段创业经历——这也是我们接下来对话的一部分——讲到你创办 PEO Partners。

turns.en: Great. Since you and I studied with Gene Fama together, no surprise that he's such an incredible thinker and teacher and you study with him and you want to do the kind of work that Gene did and you know you're not going to do it as well as he did.
turns.zh: 太好了。既然你我和我都一起师从过 Gene Fama，那他是位如此了不起的思想家和老师就不足为奇了。你跟着他学习，就会想做出 Fama 那样的工作，而你也清楚自己不可能做到像他那样好。

turns.en: It gives you a standard to strive towards and early in my career I wrote papers that were in the direction of Fama Style or Fama French Style empirical research, trying to understand what kinds of stocks outperform and to the extent that they outperform to what can we explain that with risks, can we say, well, these stocks have higher average returns because they're riskier and so it's completely rational that they perform as well
turns.zh: 但他给了你一个可以去努力追求的标准。我职业生涯早期写的一些论文，走的就是 Fama 风格、或者 Fama-French 风格的实证研究路线，试图弄清楚哪一类股票会跑赢，以及在它们跑赢的程度上，我们能否用风险来解释——我们能不能说，这些股票平均收益更高，是因为它们风险更大，所以它们表现得好是完全理性的。

turns.en: as they do. And of course, Richard Thaler, fellow Nobel Laureate along with Gene was at Chicago at the same time and Thaler argued compellingly for behavioral explanations that, hey, not everything can be explained by perfect rationality.
turns.zh: 当然了，Richard Thaler——和 Gene 同期的另一位诺贝尔奖得主——也在芝加哥。Thaler 有力地主张了行为金融学方面的解释，他说：嘿，并不是所有事情都能用完全理性来解释。

turns.en: And I'm the middle child in my family and I joke on the classic happy middle child always looking for compromise and third ways and so forth.
turns.zh: 我在家里排行中间，我常开玩笑说，典型的那种快乐的中间孩子，总是在寻找折中和第三条路之类。

turns.en: And my dissertation, I took this sort of a known puzzle, but it seems like when markets crash when they're down and the economy is down, it seems like expected returns on stocks are very high.
turns.zh: 所以我的博士论文挑了一个已经知名的谜题（puzzle），但看起来：当市场崩盘、市场下跌、经济低迷的时候，股票的预期收益似乎非常高。

turns.en: So it seems like the market in some sense goes too low and bad times and then the good times seems like the expected returns tend to be pretty low.
turns.zh: 所以市场在某种意义上似乎在坏时候跌得过低，而在好时候预期收益往往又显得相当低。

turns.en: So maybe the market got too high. Now there are risk-based explanations for this, but it could also be the people panic when things are down and then people get irrationally exuberant to use Bob Schiller's phrase when things are up high.
turns.zh: 那也许意味着市场在好的时候涨得过高了。对这种现象有基于风险的解释，但也可能是人们在市场下跌时恐慌抛售，然后在市场高企时又变得非理性地亢奋——借用 Bob Shiller 的话说，就是“非理性繁荣”（irrational exuberance）。

turns.en: But for my dissertation, I was looking for a third way solution. And so I said, maybe what happens is that if you imagine that there's two groups in the markets, there's individual investors and then there's the professional institutional investors.
turns.zh: 而在我的博士论文里，我是在寻找一个“第三条路”式的解答。于是我想，也许事情是这样的：你可以设想市场上存在两个群体——一类是个人投资者，另一类是专业的机构投资者。

turns.en: And the institutional investors, they have a boss, right? They have a job that they could be fired from. And so it might make sense that what's going on here is a classic agency problem where everybody's being rational, but the institutional investors are saying, boy, when markets are down, that's when people get fired from their job running a pension fund and or an endowment or what have you.
turns.zh: 而这些机构投资者是有老板的，对吧？他们有一份随时可能被炒的工作。所以这里很可能是这样一种情况：一个典型的代理问题（agency problem）——每个人都是理性的，但机构投资者在盘算：哎呀，当市场下跌的时候，恰恰就是管理养老金、捐赠基金之类的人被炒鱿鱼的时候。

turns.en: So I'm going to play it safe and sell down my stocks when the market's down, because that way I won't have a really bad outcome that might get me fired.
turns.zh: 所以我干脆稳妥一点，在市场下跌时减仓卖股票，因为这样一来我就不会遭遇那种可能让我被解雇的糟糕结果。

turns.en: And then I'll try to make up for it when markets are up higher or try to hold extra stocks to make up for it. And that could explain the phenomenon where the market seems to get artificially cheap at the bottom, artificially expensive at the top.
turns.zh: 然后等市场涨得比较高的时候，我再想办法补回来，或者多持有一些股票来弥补。这就能解释那种现象：市场在底部似乎被人为地压得特别便宜，在顶部似乎又被人为地抬得特别贵。

turns.en: So I really like this idea conceptually, but the data says what's in the data, not what you want it to say. And so I joked it in as a finance professor, you're the best thing you can do is create a puzzle.
turns.zh: 所以从概念上我非常喜欢这个想法，但数据是什么样就是什么样，它不会按你希望的那样说话。于是我把它当成玩笑——作为一个金融教授，你能做的最好的一件事，就是创造一个谜题。

turns.en: Because if you create a puzzle, then all legions of grad students and professors will write papers trying to explain your puzzle and you get all these citations.
turns.zh: 因为只要你造出一个谜题，就会有浩浩荡荡的研究生和教授写论文来试图解释你的谜题，你就收获一大堆引用。

turns.en: And the second best thing you can do is to solve a puzzle. You may not get as many citations because now it's not a hot issue anymore, but you get credit for figuring it out.
turns.zh: 第二好的事，是去解决一个谜题。你可能拿不到那么多引用，因为它不再是个热门话题了，但你会因为把它搞明白而获得认可。

turns.en: I did the distant third best thing, which is to deepen a puzzle. So because what I found was it was the exact opposite of what I hypothesized.
turns.zh: 而我做的是排在很后面的第三好的事——把谜题变得更难。因为我发现的结果，恰恰和我最初的假设相反。

turns.en: It's the individual investors who seem to sell too much in some sense at the bottom, the institutions who are buying from them. And again, you can explain that rationally.
turns.zh: 是个人投资者，在某种意义上似乎在底部卖得太多，而机构投资者是从他们手里买入的那一方。这你同样可以给出理性解释。

turns.en: You can say, gosh, if your stocks get hit really hard, even if you know the expected returns are super high on stocks, you're like, yeah, but I'm going to have to not pay the mortgage.
turns.zh: 你可以说：天哪，如果你的股票被砸得很惨，哪怕你知道股票的预期收益高得吓人，你也会想，是啊，可我要是再跌一次，我就还不起房贷了。

turns.en: If stocks get hit again. If I might have to pull my kid out of college or move out of my house, I can't risk that. I have to play it safe, even though I know stocks are a bargain.
turns.zh: 如果股票再被砸一次，我可能得把孩子从大学接出来、或者不得不搬家，我冒不起这个险。我得稳妥一点，哪怕明知道股票正便宜。

turns.en: I'm selling anyway. And that would be perfectly rational, but it also could be that people are panicking and selling for irrational reasons.
turns.zh: 我照样得卖。这完全可以是理性的，但同样也可能是人们在恐慌、出于非理性的原因在抛售。

turns.en: And so I would say that was my dissertation. And it kind of summarized the way I like to look at things and think about things, have a theory, try to make sense of the world, but if the data tells you something different and recognize that it's something different.
turns.zh: 所以我想说，那就是我的博士论文，它大致概括了我喜欢看待和思考问题的方式：先有一个理论，试着去理解世界，但如果数据告诉你的不一样，你要承认它确实不一样。

turns.en: So you finished your PhD, I want to say 1998. Is that correct? That's right. Okay. So you're a freshly minted university, Chicago PhD, you hit the jobs market.
turns.zh: 所以你读完博士——我想是 1998 年，对吧？——对，没错。好，那你一个 freshly minted、刚出炉的芝加哥大学博士，踏上了求职市场。

turns.en: You spent time at Harvard. You've spent time at MIT, I believe. Yeah. Walk us through your journey of teaching over the years. You focused on manager persistence, but kind of open it up a little bit.
turns.zh: 你在哈佛待过，我想你也在 MIT 待过。——是的。给我们讲讲你这些年教书的旅程吧。你研究过基金经理的持续性（manager persistence），不过不妨把话题再打开一点。

turns.en: Well, it's an embarrassing story, but I'll tell it. So what happened is I love to teach and I've always loved to teach. And I did substitute high school teaching back right after college when I was trying to start a business and just needed to make a little money.
turns.zh: 嗯，这是个挺尴尬的故事，不过我愿意讲讲。是这样的：我热爱教学，我一直都热爱教学。大学毕业后我很快就去代过高中的课，那时我正尝试创业，只是想赚点钱。

turns.en: In college, I was a teaching assistant in a computer science course. Of course, I was a chief commas TA, one of the greatest honors of my life and did that for three years.
turns.zh: 上大学时，我在一门计算机科学课上当过助教，当然，我是首席批改作业的助教，那是我人生中最高的荣誉之一，我干了三年。

turns.en: So I came to Harvard as a school with reasonable confidence that I knew how to teach and had experience and was a good teacher. So I taught the first semester and there was a student who was what they call here an ed rep.
turns.zh: 所以我带着相当足的底气来到哈佛，因为我确信自己知道怎么教书、有经验、是个好老师。我教了第一个学期，班里有一位学生，这里管她叫 ed rep，也就是教育代表。

turns.en: So educational representative in other words, she was nominated by her section, the 90 or so students who were in together in taking the class with me to be the channel of communication with the professors and tell them about issues and so forth.
turns.zh: 换句话说，她是被她所在的那个班提名的——那个班大约有 90 个学生和我一起上这门课——她的职责是充当与教授沟通的桥梁，把各种问题反馈给他们。

turns.en: And she came to me regularly during the semester to tell me things I could be doing better. Honestly, I was irritated. Like, why is this person bugging me?
turns.zh: 她在整个学期里经常来找我，告诉我哪些地方我可以做得更好。说实话，我当时挺恼火的：这人干嘛老来烦我？

turns.en: You know, I'm doing a good job. So anyway, the end of the semester comes and the students fill out a form. They rate us from one to seven in a bunch of categories, but there's an overall rating.
turns.zh: 你知道嘛，我觉得自己干得挺好。不管怎样，学期结束时，学生要填一张表，他们在若干类别上给我们从 1 到 7 打分，另外还有一个总体评分。

turns.en: And back then it was on paper now, of course, it's digital. And I got the piece of paper. And so of course, I'm eager to see, I didn't I see that I got 6.2 out of seven.
turns.zh: 那时候还是纸质的，现在当然都数字化了。我拿到那张纸。我当然迫不及待地想看看——我看到我得了 6.2 分（满分 7 分）。

turns.en: And I thought, okay, I'd like to do better in the long run. Certainly not terrible for first time out of the box. I felt okay about, but then I realized, oh, wait, I'm looking at the wrong side of the page.
turns.zh: 我心想，好吧，长远看我还想做得更好，但第一次教书这肯定不算糟。我觉得还行。可随后我意识到：等等，我看的是页错的那一面。

turns.en: This is the course average. I need to flip the page over to see my score. My score was 2.6 out of seven. And then I had the most horrifying realization of my life.
turns.zh: 那是这门课的平均分。我得把纸翻过来才能看到我自己的分数。我的分数是 2.6 分（满分 7 分）。然后我经历了人生中最可怕的一次顿悟。

turns.en: The course average included me. So the people who weren't me teaching introductory finance, first year finances, it was called at the time average 6.7 out of seven.
turns.zh: 这门课的平均分里还包括了我自己。也就是说，那些不是我的人在教入门金融——当时那门课就叫大一金融——平均分是 6.7 分（满分 7 分）。

turns.en: And that included other rookies. And they averaged 6.7. So the course was so good that even rookies were coming in and getting 6.5, 6.7. And I'm at 2.6.
turns.zh: 这里面还包含其他新手老师。他们平均能拿 6.7。所以这门课教得如此之好，以至于连新手进来都能拿 6.5、6.7。而我却只有 2.6。

turns.en: So first of all, I just want to say, obviously, I won't say her name, but to the woman, if she ever hears this, who was the ad rep in that class, I salute you.
turns.zh: 所以首先我想说的是，我当然不会提她的名字，但那位在那门课上担任教育代表的女士——如果她哪天听到这段——向你致敬。

turns.en: Because it took a lot of guts for her to come. And she tried to tell me that I was screwing up and I didn't want to hear it. I was grading her, right?
turns.zh: 因为她当初来找我有很大勇气。她试图告诉我我搞砸了，而我不想听。我当时还在给她打分呢，对吧？

turns.en: So it was totally bold of her to tell me the truth. And I thank her for it. And I wish I'd listened more. It was a lesson for me. And so then I went and one of my colleagues here did an amazing thing.
turns.zh: 所以她把真话告诉我，是非常大胆的。我为此感谢她。我真希望当时能多听进去一些。那对我是一个教训。后来我的一个同事在这里做了件了不起的事。

turns.en: There was a group here called the Derek Bach Center on Teaching and Learning, which is for the faculty of arts and sciences at Harvard. Derek was the president of Harvard back actually when I went as an undergrad.
turns.zh: 这里有一个叫 Derek Bok 教学与学习中心（Derek Bok Center on Teaching and Learning）的机构，它是为哈佛文理学院的教授们服务的。Derek 当年担任哈佛校长的时候，我正好作为本科生在那里。

turns.en: And the thing is that Harvard Business School professors were not allowed to benefit from this resource because Harvard has this 400 year tradition, which in the slang of the 1600s is every tub on its own bottom, which I guess is sort of like every man for itself or himself or herself.
turns.zh: 问题是，哈佛商学院的教授本来是不允许享受这个资源的，因为哈佛有一个延续 400 年的传统，用 1600 年代的行话说叫“every tub on its own bottom”（每个桶都浮在自己的底上），我猜大意就是各人自扫门前雪。

turns.en: So each of the schools at Harvard is independent in their finances and so forth. So this was something for the faculty of arts and sciences, for the physics department and the English department, not for HBS.
turns.zh: 所以哈佛的每个学院在财务等方面都是各自独立的。因此这个中心是给文理学院的教授用的，给物理系、英语系用的，不是给 HBS 用的。

turns.en: But my colleague pulled strings and got me in there and they were amazing. And they taught me so much that I didn't know about teaching. But I'll tell you the single most important thing I learned.
turns.zh: 但我的同事托关系把我塞了进去，那边真的太棒了。他们教会了我太多关于教学我原本不知道的东西。不过我要告诉你，我学到的最重要的一件事是——

turns.en: And it's funny, I say it in a jokey way to my kids. I say there are very few problems in life that can't be solved with 100 hours of hard work.
turns.zh: 说来好笑，我用开玩笑的口吻对我的孩子说：人生里很少有问题是花 100 小时下苦功解决不了的。

turns.en: And the fact is I was prepping maybe two or three hours for each class and I needed to be prepping 10 or 20 hours for each class. Not, of course, not forever.
turns.zh: 而事实是，我当时每上一节课大概只备课两三个小时，而我本该每节课备上 10 到 20 个小时。当然，不是一辈子都这样。

turns.en: Like the first time through and then the next time was a little less. But I just needed to be so much deeper in my knowledge. But there were other things too that I needed to over and turned it around in one year.
turns.zh: 就是头一遍要这样，下一遍就能少一些。但我确实需要在知识的深度上下 much more 功夫。而且还有很多别的东西我也需要改进，我在一年之内就把局面扭转了过来。

turns.en: And by the way, now we have the Christensen Center here at HBS. And I like to think that I might have played a tiny inspirational role in them, creating that because they after the great click, Christensen, my former colleague.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，现在我们 HBS 有了 Christensen 中心。我愿意相信，我在他们创立这个中心时可能起到了一点点启发作用，因为那是以伟大的 Clayton Christensen、我的前同事命名的。

turns.en: And so anyway, I taught intro finance for years. Then I taught the investments class, investment management that was created, I think by Jay Light, our former dean, he passed it on to Andre Peril, who was my mentor.
turns.zh: 所以，反正我教了好多年入门金融。后来我又教了投资管理（investment management）这门课，它是我记得是由我们的前院长 Jay Light 创建的，他把它交给了 André Perold，那是我的导师。

turns.en: Jay was also a great mentor and Andre was nice enough to allow me to take the course over. And I taught that for a number of years. And then when I moved to MIT, I went and I brought that class to MIT.
turns.zh: Jay 也是一位伟大的导师，André 也好心地允许我把这门课接下来。我教了好几年。后来我去了 MIT，就把这门课也带去了 MIT。

turns.en: And that was new at MIT because I was teaching case method, which is not widely used at MIT and not widely used at most schools. Of course, it wasn't used at Chicago, really, when we were there in any major way.
turns.zh: 这在 MIT 是新鲜的，因为我用的是案例教学法（case method），这在 MIT 并不普遍使用，在大多数学校也不普遍。当然，我们在芝加哥那会儿，芝加哥基本也不怎么用它。

turns.en: And first year teaching at MIT, I won the teacher year award, not because I'm such a brilliant teacher, you know, probably not the top half of teachers at HBS.
turns.zh: 我在 MIT 教书的第一年，就赢得了年度教师奖，这并不是因为我是多么了不起的老师——你知道，我在 HBS 大概连教师的前一半都排不进。

turns.en: But because it's classic efficient frontier, I was extending the frontiers, giving the students a form of learning that they weren't getting enough of.
turns.zh: 而是因为这是经典的“有效前沿”（efficient frontier）：我在拓展前沿，给学生提供了一种他们原本得不到的学习形式。

turns.en: So I think that really was great. But it was a great experience for me. And I taught at MIT for a number of years, taught investments. And last piece of this, sorry, I'm not logging too much, is that I have a degenerative eye condition, retinitis pigmentosa, and so I've been slowly going blind my whole life.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得那真的很好，对我来说也是一段很棒经历。我在 MIT 教了好几年，教投资管理。还有最后一点，抱歉，我讲得有点长了——我有一种退行性的眼疾，叫视网膜色素变性（retinitis pigmentosa），所以我这辈子一直在慢慢变盲。

turns.en: And when I went to teach at MIT, I had unbelievably bad eyesight. But by the time I came back to HBS six years later, I was sort of a blind guy who could see a tiny bit.
turns.zh: 我当年去 MIT 教书的时候，视力已经差得离谱。等我六年之后回到 HBS 时，我已经算是个只能看见一点点光的盲人了。

turns.en: And it turned out I couldn't really teach the HBS case method anymore while being that blind. And so I really had to scramble to come up with something that I could teach blind.
turns.zh: 结果发现，在那么瞎的情况下，我其实没法再教 HBS 的案例教学了。所以我不得不拼命赶紧想出一个我作为盲人也能教的课程。

turns.en: And the HBS was incredibly supportive of me. And I was able to develop a course called FieldX, which is a course for startup businesses. And that's what I've been teaching the last decade.
turns.zh: HBS 对我支持得无以复加。我最终开发出了一门叫 FieldX 的课，是一门为初创企业开设的课。这就是我过去十年一直在教的东西。

turns.en: And essentially, it's an incubator for companies being formed at HBS and also other parts of Harvard and surrounding schools. We've had wonderful schools from Tufts and MIT, excuse me, wonderful students from Tufts and MIT and other schools.
turns.zh: 它本质上是一个孵化器，孵化那些在 HBS 以及在哈佛其他学院和周边学校正在成立的公司。我们也接收过来自塔夫茨大学（Tufts）和 MIT 的优秀学生——抱歉——来自 Tufts 和 MIT 以及其他学校的优秀学生。

turns.en: And students from the law school and graduate school of design and so forth, but mostly HBS. And this semester, for example, we have 73 teams in the class who are starting at the city, they're 73 real businesses.
turns.zh: 还有法学院、设计研究生院等的学生，但主要还是 HBS。举个例子，这个学期我们有 73 个团队在上课，他们正在起步——在城里创业，他们做的是 73 家真实的公司。

turns.en: Now, they will all raise money and become full-time jobs after graduation. But based on recent history, probably half or more of them will. And the rest will just be great student projects, which is also wonderful.
turns.zh: 这些团队里，将来都会有人融资，并在毕业后把它变成全职事业。但根据近几年的历史，大概有一半或更多会真的这么干。剩下的就会是很棒的学生项目，那也同样精彩。

turns.en: So sorry, that was a little longer than you probably wanted, but that's my teaching journey. Well, the learning from early, I don't call them mistakes, but just areas where you can improve and taking a critical view of where you can do that.
turns.zh: 抱歉，我可能讲得比你想要的长了一点，但这就是我教书的旅程。——嗯，从一开始就学习，我不会把它们叫作错误，而是可以改进的地方，用批判的眼光去看自己在哪些方面还能提升。

turns.en: And I love the concept of I was putting in two to three hours and I need to be putting in ten. That's a really interesting and straightforward thing that you, as you said, you're in control of that.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢那个“我原来只花两三个小时、而我本该花十个小时”的说法，这真是既有趣又直接的一点——正如你所说，这件事是你能掌控的。

turns.en: You mentioned teaching investment management. And so, well, gosh, if we go back to the 80s and 90s, you had your capital markets line. You had consistently positive interest rates.
turns.zh: 你提到了教投资管理。那么，如果我们回到 80 年代和 90 年代，那时候你有你的资本市场线（capital markets line），利率一直是正的、而且很稳定。

turns.en: You didn't have just derivative products. You certainly didn't have central banks putting their thumb on the scales and telling you the policy rate is going to be negative 50 basis points for years.
turns.zh: 那时候没有这么多衍生产品，当然更没有央行把自己的拇指按在秤上、告诉你政策利率未来几年都要维持在负 50 个基点。

turns.en: So what does investment management as a professor at a business school, what does that class look like versus what it might look like when I was at the GSB with you?
turns.zh: 所以作为一名商学院教授，投资管理这门课上起来是什么样子？和我当年在 GSB 跟你同学时，它看起来会有什么不同？

turns.en: Yeah, it is funny. Every time something crazy happens in the world, of course, finance professors were human beings and we think about pain that may be caused to people who lose money or lose their jobs or have difficult situations to face.
turns.zh: 是啊，挺有意思的。每当世界上发生什么疯狂的事，金融教授当然也是人，我们会想到那些亏钱、失业、或面对艰难处境的人所承受的痛苦。

turns.en: But there's a tiny part of us like, wow, this is a fascinating natural experiment. We've never had negative people used to talk about whether, you know, negative real interest rates were something that could really happen.
turns.zh: 但我们身上也有一小部分在想：哇，这真是一个迷人的自然实验（natural experiment）。我们以前还讨论负的实际利率是不是真能发生那种事。

turns.en: We got native nominal interest rates. Nobody saw that coming. I won't say nobody there. Of course, it was research thinking through the circumstances under which there are currently a lot of smart people in the profession.
turns.zh: 结果我们得到了负的名义利率，谁都没料到。我不敢说完全“没人料到”——当然，那之前就有研究在思考在什么样的条件下会出现这种情形，而现在行业里有很多聪明人在琢磨它。

turns.en: But when it happened, it was a stunner and it was again, obviously, it was all part of some really bad stuff that was happening that grew into a lot of lives.
turns.zh: 但当它真的发生时，它还是让人震惊。而且这当然又是那些糟糕事情的一部分，它蔓延开来、影响了很多人的生活。

turns.en: And that is awful. But from a pure research perspective to see something new is so interesting. Of course, we've seen so many new things over the years, whether it's the negative interest rates, whether it's the rise of crypto and the role it's played in markets, whether it is just the enormous scale that private equities achieved.
turns.zh: 那很糟糕。但从纯粹研究的角度看，能见证一些全新的东西，实在太有意思了。这些年我们当然见过太多新鲜事——负利率也好，加密资产（crypto）的崛起及其在市场中所扮演的角色也好，还是私募股权所达到的惊人规模也好。

turns.en: And now the efforts to make private equity part of everybody's portfolio rather than just big institutions and the ultra wealthy. There's always something new and fascinating.
turns.zh: 再到如今想把私募股权变成每个人组合的一部分，而不再只属于大型机构超级富豪——总有一些新的、迷人的东西在出现。

turns.en: And I'll come back to your negative interest rate point in the back of my brain. I'm trying to think of something interesting to say about that.
turns.zh: 关于负利率那点，我会再回来谈。我脑子里正在拼命想，好对那点说点有意思的话。

turns.en: But let me just say that people will sometimes say to me, look, Brandy, isn't asset management going to be dead because people get smarter, the computers get better, aren't we just going to get more and more rational at figuring out where there are mispricings and they just get fixed quicker and quicker.
turns.zh: 不过我先说，人们有时会问我：Randy，资产管理这行难道不会“死掉”吗？因为人们越来越聪明、电脑越来越强，我们不是会越来越理性地找出定价错误、让错误被更快更快地修正吗？

turns.en: And you and I are friends, even with some of the smartest people out there working on fixing those mispricings. And some of them have gotten a very large scale and can trade jillions a day and all that. How are the opportunities going to survive?
turns.zh: 你和我那些朋友——即便是最聪明的一批人，也在忙着修正这些错误定价——他们当中一些已经做到非常大的规模，一天能交易天文数字般的量。那机会怎么可能还存活下来？

turns.en: And what I've come to realize is because there's always something new. And so maybe the US large caps become very efficiently priced. Maybe they have already or maybe not already, but maybe they will at some point.
turns.zh: 而我逐渐意识到的是：正因为总有新东西出现。所以也许美国大盘股会变得非常有效地定价。也许它们已经有效了，也许还没有，但也许某一刻会。

turns.en: But then maybe there are opportunities in China because you kept short in China and therefore that creates certain kinds of mispricings. And then maybe there is an opportunity in Pakistan because the market in Pakistan wasn't even something you could realistically invest in as a US asset manager, but then circumstances change as you can.
turns.zh: 但接着，也许中国有机会，因为你在中国的空头头寸带来了某类错误定价；然后也许巴基斯坦有机会，因为巴基斯坦的市场过去根本不是一个美国资产管理人现实上能投的东西，但环境会变，你能投了。

turns.en: And then people invent new derivatives and now there's markets in those derivatives and you've got the crypto. And oh my gosh, I didn't even think yet to mention the prediction markets and all the stuff that's going on there.
turns.zh: 然后人们发明了新的衍生品，于是这些衍生品也形成了市场；再有你看到了加密资产——天哪，我甚至还没提到预测市场（prediction markets），以及那边正在发生的种种。

turns.en: So the point is new things come along and I do think there is a story where anything new that comes along starts off as a very inefficient market and works its way over time to be more efficient.
turns.zh: 所以要点在于：新东西不断出现，而且我确实认为有一个这样的规律——任何新出现的东西，一开始都是一个非常低效的市场，然后随着时间推移逐渐变得更有效。

turns.en: You think of something like convertible arbitrage where my sense is that for people who got into that back in the 1990s, there was some pretty easy money to be made in convertible arbitrage.
turns.zh: 你想想可转换套利（convertible arbitrage）这类东西。我的感觉是，对 90 年代就进入那行的人而言，在可转换套利里曾经能赚到相当轻松的钱。

turns.en: People are still running convertible arbitrage funds and still doing it well. But I don't think anybody would say it's easy money. They got to work their tail off to squeeze out some alpha for their investor.
turns.zh: 现在仍有人在做可转换套利基金、而且做得不错。但我想没人会说那是轻松的钱了。他们得拼了命才能为自己的投资人榨出一点 alpha。

turns.en: So things change over time. In terms of the interest rates going native, it really was fascinating because our intuition plays us false, right?
turns.zh: 所以事情会随时间变化。说到利率转负，那真的很有意思，因为我们的直觉骗了我们，对吧？

turns.en: In other words, there were things that seemed like obviously it must be a great investment to short these bonds. They're paying you to borrow money, essentially.
turns.zh: 换句话说，有些事情看起来显然地——做空这些债券肯定是很棒的投资，等于是别人付钱请你来借钱。

turns.en: And then it turned out not necessarily, it turned out that people would say, look, it's gone a little below zero, can't go much more than that.
turns.zh: 然后结果证明不一定如此。人们会说：哦，它只跌到零利率下面一点点，不可能再往下多少。

turns.en: And then sometimes it would go very negative. So I think it was really intellectually valuable to have our intuitions tested and pushed and see the different kinds of things that happened and open our minds to stuff. I'll just tell one more quick story, which is my colleague, Mark Mitchell, got very interested.
turns.zh: 然后有时候它又会变得非常负。所以我觉得，让我们的直觉受到检验、被推着走、看到各种各样发生的事情、从而打开思路，在智识上非常有价值。我再讲一个短故事，就是我的同事 Mark Mitchell，他对一件东西变得非常感兴趣。

turns.en: Now he's a big asset manager, but he's my professor at Chicago PhD. He might have had him too. And then he came and joined me at HBS. So we taught here together for a number of years and he wanted to write a paper on the POM 3.com thing, right?
turns.zh: 他现在是一位大型资产管理人，但他在芝加哥读博时是我的导师。你也许也上过他的课。后来他来到 HBS 和我一起，我们在这里一起教了好几年。他想就 Palm 和 3Com 那件事写一篇论文，对吧？

turns.en: So you'll remember this, that POM had this or sorry, 3.com was a company that basically made computer modems and then they had a division that created the POM pilot, which was this proto iPhone device that people loved.
turns.zh: 你还会记得，——抱歉，3Com 是一家公司，基本上是做电脑调制解调器的，然后他们有个部门做出了 Palm Pilot，那是一种 iPhone 出现之前的原型手持设备，人们特别喜爱它。

turns.en: And it was really neat, this handheld device. It could do all kinds of cool stuff and they spun out the company POM, but they kept the majority of the company and POM became a super hot tech stock.
turns.zh: 那玩意儿真的很酷，一个手持设备，能做各种很炫的事。他们把 Palm 这家公司分拆了出去，但保留了大部分股权，而 Palm 成了一只超级热门的科技股。

turns.en: And the price got very high and the thing was that the price of 3.com, which owned most of POM, didn't get that high because there were people buying POM who didn't understand the 3.com owned most of it and so that they could have effectively bought POM cheaper by buying 3.com.
turns.zh: Palm 的价格涨得很高，而持有 Palm 大部分股份的 3Com 的价格却没有涨那么高，因为有些买 Palm 的人并不清楚 3Com 拥有 Palm 的大部分，所以他们本可以通过买 3Com 来间接更便宜地买到 Palm。

turns.en: And then you get POM, big parts of POM in the market. So then there was an arbitrage trade where you said, OK, we're going to buy the cheap stock 3.com.
turns.zh: 也就是说，通过 3Com 你能得到 Palm 很大一块股份。于是这就存在一个套利交易：好，我们去买便宜的股票 3Com。

turns.en: We're going to short POM and it should be locked in profits because you have to sell it and Mark decided to write a paper about all these situations of this type because it turned out there were a whole bunch of them in the market at that time.
turns.zh: 然后我们去卖空 Palm，这应该是锁定利润的交易，因为最终它会收敛。而 Mark 决定就这一类情形写一篇论文，因为事实证明当时市场上有一大堆这样的情形。

turns.en: And what he did, he said, you know what, I'm never going to really understand all the things that can go wrong unless I actually go buy these.
turns.zh: 而他做的一件事是：他说，你知道吗，除非我真的去买这些，否则我永远没法真正理解所有可能出错的地方。

turns.en: So he took a little of his own money and he went and he bought, did every one of these trades in his own account and then he discovered all the crazy stuff that could happen, like, for example, the parent company, the 3.com in this situation, could buy back stock or even the whole of the subsidiary at a price higher than its trading cost, causing you to lose on both sides of the trade.
turns.zh: 所以他拿了一点自己的钱，去把这些交易每一种都在他自己的账户里做了一遍。然后他发现了所有可能发生的疯狂状况，比如母公司——这里就是 3Com——可能回购股票，甚至可能以一个高于其交易价格的价位回购整个子公司，让你在这个交易的两头都亏钱。

turns.en: And you just had to be in it to see this stuff. And so lived experience is really important. So interesting. And that's an interesting example.
turns.zh: 你得亲自下场，才能看到这些东西。所以亲身经历（lived experience）真的很重要。——太有意思了，这是个很有意思的例子。

turns.en: I know the borrow was very compromised in that as well. You had to short sell the POM side and that was very difficult to do. Very expensive.
turns.zh: 我知道在那桩交易里，融券（borrow）也非常受限。你不得不去卖空 Palm 那一侧，而那非常难做到、非常贵。

turns.en: That's right. And that's another problem that would be these cases where you would be buying companies that were poorly run companies, but they were trading for less than the cash on the balance sheet and you're like, how can I lose?
turns.zh: 没错。还有另一类问题就是这样的情形：你在买一些经营得很烂的公司，但它们的市值低于资产负债表上的现金，你想：这怎么可能亏钱？

turns.en: And then the company would spend that cash on something that you're like, you cannot possibly be spending on this, but they did. And then they discovered you could lose.
turns.zh: 然后那家公司就把那笔现金花在某个你觉得“绝不可能拿去花在这上面”的东西上，但他们就是这么花了。然后人们就发现，原来你确实会亏钱。

turns.en: So markets are really complicated and you got to learn all the stuff. And obviously this is why we read our Matt Levine and we do all these things to keep up because there's always something new happening.
turns.zh: 所以市场真的很复杂，你得当心所有这些把戏。这显然就是我们为什么要读 Matt Levine 的文章、要做这些功课去紧跟动态的原因，因为总有新东西在发生。

turns.en: You've used the term puzzles. And I think that's a very good term. So there's so many of these, the equity premium puzzle, the forward rate puzzle on the FX side.
turns.zh: 你用了“谜题”（puzzles）这个词，我觉得这是个很好的词。有太多这样的谜题了——股权溢价谜题（equity premium puzzle）、外汇那边的远期利率谜题（forward rate puzzle）。

turns.en: There's a number of these. There was at least for a time, there was the January effect. I don't know if that's really still there. Cliff says he doesn't really believe as much in the size effect anymore.
turns.zh: 有这么一些。至少曾经有一段时间，还有一月效应（January effect），我不知道它现在是否真的还在。Cliff 说他不太再那么相信规模效应（size effect）了。

turns.en: It that's accounted for through other factors. What are some of the puzzles that you find to be the biggest ones in markets? If you were to just to cite one or two of them that you wrestle with.
turns.zh: 它被其他因子解释了。那么，在你看来，市场里最大的几个谜题是什么？如果只让你列出一两个你一直在与之较量的谜题。

turns.en: And then also over time. And again, just to bring Cliff as this back into it, you know, he said over time, he says, I find markets a little less efficient, which I think is an interesting statement. So we're always watching things and updating our views.
turns.zh: 还有随时间的变化。再说一次，把 Cliff 带回来——你知道，他说随着时间推移，他觉得市场没那么有效了，我觉得这是个很有意思的说法。所以我们一直在观察、在更新自己的看法。

turns.en: Take us through one or two of these puzzles and how your thought process on them has evolved over time. We can think of things in a range from puzzles where there's a pretty decent rational explanation. It doesn't mean it's right, but at least it fits.
turns.zh: 带我们走查一两个这样的谜题，以及你在这上面的思考过程随时间是怎么演变的。——我们可以把谜题放在一个谱系里来看：一端是有相当不错的理性解释的谜题，这不代表解释对，但至少它讲得通。

turns.en: And it could be right. And then at the other end, you have things where it's like, OK, obviously, this is a behavioral error. And generally those that latter category is things that are that are pretty small.
turns.zh: 而且它有可能是对的。而在另一端，有些东西就是那种“显然这是一个行为错误”。通常那后一类，都是相对较小的效应。

turns.en: And when you think about the most interesting stuff, if I were to look at a puzzle that is and then let me add that in terms of rational explanations, you might say that rational behavior, there's even a spectrum there.
turns.zh: 当你思考最有意思的那些东西时，如果我要挑一个既算谜题、那么我再补充一点：就理性解释而言，即便是理性行为本身也存在一个谱系。

turns.en: So let's talk about momentum for a second. I actually wrote a case with Cliff's team on AQR's Momentum Fund, which is one of my favorite cases that I wrote because I thought I was writing a boring case and it turned out to be super interesting.
turns.zh: 我们先说说动量（momentum）吧。其实我和 Cliff 的团队一起写过一个关于 AQR 动量基金（AQR's Momentum Fund）的案例，那是我写过的案例里我最喜欢的之一，因为我本以为我在写一个无聊的案例，结果它变得超级有意思。

turns.en: So what happened is that as you're well aware, there's a historically been what people call the momentum effect in stock return. And generally people summarize as two to twelve.
turns.zh: 事情是这样的，你也很清楚，历史上存在人们所说的股票收益中的动量效应。人们通常把它总结为 2 到 12 个月。

turns.en: They say the most recent month, the winners tend to go down and the losers tend to go up. So one month reversal. But if you focus on the last year, ignoring the most recent month, then it seems like the stocks that went up over that period continue to go up subsequently.
turns.zh: 他们说：最近一个月的表现会反转——赢家往往往下走，输家往往往上走，也就是一个月的反转。但如果你把过去一年的区间拿来看、忽略最近那一个月，那么在这段时间里上涨的股票，之后似乎会继续上涨。

turns.en: So one thing about levels of rationality is there's a story that says this is an overreaction effect. And so that goes that you have a stock and it does well.
turns.zh: 所以关于“理性程度”的层次，有一个说法是：这是一种过度反应（overreaction）效应。故事是这样的：你有一只股票，它表现好。

turns.en: They have good news. And so then the stock goes up and that's like instant good news stock jumps. And then you get a bunch of like newspaper articles and they do magazine articles about the CEO and how smart they are and all these stuff.
turns.zh: 它有好的消息。于是股票上涨，就像即时的好消息让股价一跳。然后涌出一堆报纸文章、杂志文章，讲这位 CEO 有多聪明之类。

turns.en: And then people who weren't paying attention when news was announced, say, well, that stock sounds really good and they buy it and they push it up above fair of out, right?
turns.zh: 然后那些在消息公布时没在关注的人就说：哇，那只股票听起来真不错，于是他们买入，把股价推到公允价值之上，对吧？

turns.en: So say they had 10 percent of good news, it jumps 10 percent and then it jumps another 3 percent over the subsequent year as people who weren't on top of the initial thing buy it.
turns.zh: 假设它出了 10% 的好消息，股价先跳 10%，然后在随后一年里又涨 3%，因为那些没第一时间跟上的人陆续买入。

turns.en: OK, so that's the overreaction story for momentum. Now, then there's an underreaction story for momentum. The underreaction story, I'll tell this one on the downside, but both of these stories apply in both directions, but I joke about this with my dad.
turns.zh: 好，这是动量的过度反应故事。接下来还有动量的反应不足（underreaction）故事。反应不足的故事，我从下行那面来讲，但这两个故事在两个方向上都成立。我跟我爸开这个玩笑。

turns.en: My dad likes to invest in stocks sometimes and he'll watch the financial news and he'll be like, look, they just missed their earnings by a penny.
turns.zh: 我爸有时候喜欢投资股票，他会看财经新闻，然后会说：你看，他们每股收益只是差了一美分没达到预期。

turns.en: And the stock dropped 5 percent. It's crazy. It's a buying opportunity. And of course, we know there's a momentum effect. There's a momentum effect and there's earnings moment.
turns.zh: 而股价跌了 5%，太疯狂了，这是个买入良机啊。而我们当然知道存在动量效应，也有盈利动量（earnings momentum）。

turns.en: If you have bad news about earnings, it tends to drop not enough. So the underreaction effect would say, hey, there's 10 percent of bad news.
turns.zh: 如果你在盈利上有坏消息，股价往往跌得还不够。所以反应不足效应会说：嘿，有 10% 的坏消息。

turns.en: The stock only goes down seven because people like my dad are buying on the dip and they're actually not letting it fall and then address the other 3 percent down over the rest of the year.
turns.zh: 而股价只跌了 7%，因为像我爸那样的人在逢低买入，他们其实没让它跌到位，剩下的另外 3% 的跌幅，是在这一年的剩余时间里慢慢补上的。

turns.en: Now, let me assist you and I don't think there's a definitive answer to this. What does your gut tell you? Is momentum an underreaction or an overreaction?
turns.zh: 那么，我想反问你，而我也不觉得这里有确定答案——你的直觉告诉你，动量是反应不足还是过度反应？

turns.en: I think it's an underreaction. I like underreaction. You know why I think you and I like that because underreaction is like it's almost rational.
turns.zh: 我觉得是反应不足。——我喜欢反应不足。你知道为什么我觉得我们俩都偏爱它吗？因为反应不足几乎是理性的。

turns.en: Do you know what I mean? It's like an almost rational story. You just took a little time to get there. The overreaction story is a crazier rational story.
turns.zh: 你明白我的意思吗？它就像一个“近乎理性”的故事：你只是花了一点时间才到位。而过度反应的故事是一个更不“讲理性”的故事。

turns.en: And you and I are tempted by the story, the close to rationality, even the full rationality won't get us there. Now, I don't know if we're right or not.
turns.zh: 你和我都被那个“接近理性”的说法吸引。即便完全理性也到不了那里。不过我也不知道我们俩对不对。

turns.en: The last time I looked into this, it seemed like the evidence for overreaction was a little better, but that may have changed in the five years since I looked at it or I may have misinterpreted the research.
turns.zh: 我上一次深入研究这事时，看起来过度反应的证据稍微好一点点，但那可能在我看过之后的五年里已经变了，也可能是我误读了那些研究。

turns.en: OK, now here's what happened with the AQR's momentum fund. So AQR had been trading hedge funds. They've been trading these momentum strategies for many years.
turns.zh: 好，那 AQR 的动量基金后来发生了什么。AQR 一直在做对冲基金，他们做了很多年的这类动量策略。

turns.en: Written great papers on the subject and so forth. And what happened is that they decided to launch a mutual fund based on momentum. Now, since it was a mutual fund, it's going to be long only.
turns.zh: 就这个话题写过很棒的论文，等等。所发生的是，他们决定基于动量发起一只共同基金（mutual fund）。既然是共同基金，那它就是只做多的（long only）。

turns.en: So you wouldn't be both buying the winners and selling losers. You just be on one side. My view was, OK, this would be a case where I could teach the students, first of all, that there's a momentum effect and what the history was on it.
turns.zh: 所以你不会一边买赢家、一边卖输家，你只站在其中一边。我的看法是：好，这可以成为这样一个案例，让我能教学生——第一，存在动量效应，以及它的历史是怎样的。

turns.en: And second, I could teach them about forming a mutual fund and how you do that. And they did a clever thing where they created an index because you can't use a back test in marketing a mutual fund.
turns.zh: 第二，我能教他们怎么组建一只共同基金、具体怎么做。他们做了件聪明的事，就是创建了一个指数，因为你不能拿回测（back test）去营销一只共同基金。

turns.en: But if you create an index, you can show the index results. So they created the AQR momentum index to accompany the fund. So it was all really smart.
turns.zh: 但如果你创建一个指数，你就可以展示这个指数的表现。于是他们创建了 AQR 动量指数，配合那只基金。所以这一切都非常聪明。

turns.en: Obviously, they do things really well at that firm. And it was well thought out. So we're going to end, I have three wonderful co-authors on that case, my colleagues here.
turns.zh: 显然，那家公司做事做得很好，而且考虑得很周全。我们讲到哪了？我那篇案例有三个很棒的合著者，都是我在这里的同事。

turns.en: OK, so we write the case, then we finish the case around the end of 2008 or something like that. And then I teach the case for the first time in 2009.
turns.zh: 好，我们写这个案例，大约在 2008 年底左右把它写完。然后我在 2009 年第一次教这个案例。

turns.en: And the basic finding of the case is, if you go along the top momentum decile and short the bottom momentum decile, you made about 15% a year.
turns.zh: 这个案例的基本发现是：如果你做多动量十分位最高的一组、做空最低的一组，你一年大约能赚 15%。

turns.en: And the data went back 80 years. OK, so 80 years of 15% a year. So I have the students talk about it and they're like this. And I pulled them.
turns.zh: 而数据往回有 80 年。好，那就是 80 年、每年 15%。我让学生讨论这个，他们一脸惊叹，我逗他们。

turns.en: I'm like, what do you think? And they're like, yes, it's amazing. Everybody, every hand goes up. It's great. OK, so then I say, well, let's look and see how momentum did in 2009.
turns.zh: 我说，你们怎么想？他们说：天哪，太神奇了。每个人都举手。太好了。然后我说：好，我们来看看动量在 2009 年表现如何。

turns.en: OK, and then I show the results. And the result is that if you were along the top decile, short the bottom decile in 2009, do you know what the returns were?
turns.zh: 然后我展示结果。结果是：如果你在 2009 年做多最高十分位、做空最低十分位，你知道收益是多少吗？

turns.en: You want to say yes? I'm going to say remarkably bad. Remarkably, that is correct. Minus one hundred and twenty percent. Yeah. OK, was that the dash for trash period?
turns.zh: 你想说是吗？我可以说——糟得离谱。——糟得离谱。没错。是负 120%。——是啊。——哦，那是“奔向垃圾”（dash for trash）那段时间吗？

turns.en: Well, the way to think of it is remember Citibank Citigroup traded down to 99 cents, if memory serves, and it went up to four dollars. That's three hundred percent against you in this trade.
turns.zh: 这么理解吧：还记得花旗银行、Citigroup 跌到了 99 美分，如果我没记错的话，然后它涨到了 4 美元。在这个交易里，光这一只就对你反着来了 300%。

turns.en: All those financials that were down to about snapback. And so you lost one hundred and twenty percent now is unbelievable. So then I say, students, what do you think of momentum now?
turns.zh: 所有那些金融股都在暴跌之后反弹。所以你亏了 120%，这太难以置信了。然后我问学生：现在你们怎么看动量？

turns.en: And they're like, well, it's terrible. You lost all your money and more. I'm like, OK, well, let's compute the average return over the 81 years.
turns.zh: 他们说：嗯，它糟透了。你把钱全亏了还倒欠。我说：好，那我们把 81 年里的平均收益算一算。

turns.en: I'm like, is anyone good at doing this stuff in their head? Of course, someone is right. 80 times plus 15 plus one times minus 120 is plus 13 and a half.
turns.zh: 我说，谁能在心里算这个？当然有人能。80 次正 15%，加上一次负 120%，除以 81，等于正 13.5%。

turns.en: I'm like, this strategy makes 13 and a half percent a year. What's so terrible about that? But like, but all your money's gone. I'm like, OK, so let's think this through.
turns.zh: 我说，这个策略一年能赚 13.5%，那有什么好可怕的？——可是他们：可你的钱全没了啊。我说：好，那我们把这事想清楚。

turns.en: So then what it turns out is that if you put your money into 10 strategies, one of which is momentum 100 years ago or 81 years ago, then what would have happened is the momentum one would have had the vast majority of the money because it did so unbelievably well.
turns.zh: 结果发现，如果你在 100 年前、或者 81 年前，把钱分成 10 个策略，其中一个是动量，那么会发生的是：动量那个策略会占据绝大部分的资金，因为它表现得难以置信地好。

turns.en: And then you'd have lost it all. And so it would be a devastating blow. But on the other hand, if you put money into the 10 different strategies and then every year you rebalance.
turns.zh: 然后你会把它全亏掉。那会是一记毁灭性的重击。但另一方面，如果你把钱分成 10 个不同策略，然后每一年都再平衡（rebalance）。

turns.en: So at the beginning of each year, you were a tenth in each. But yeah, you lose 12 percent across the portfolio, a tenth of 120. But combined with all the amazing years, it's fine.
turns.zh: 也就是每年年初你在每个策略上各放十分之一。没错，你整个组合亏 12%，即十分之一的 120。但把它和所有那些出色的年份合在一起，就没问题了。

turns.en: And so this turns out to be all about geometric averages versus our arithmetic averages and about computing IRRs versus there. And so there's all these deep lessons in here, none of which I expected.
turns.zh: 所以这最终关乎几何平均（geometric average）与算术平均（arithmetic average）之别，关乎计算 IRR 还是别的。这里面有好多深刻的教训，而我当初写案例时一个都没料到。

turns.en: When I wrote the case, but it just gives you an idea of all the different angles that come from one of these things. Let me just to give you the other side of the spectrum, say a word about an extreme obvious puzzle.
turns.zh: 这也让你看到，从这样一件事里能衍生出多少不同的角度。让我再举一个处在谱系另一端的例子，说说一个极端的、明显的谜题。

turns.en: So there is a lot of history of name confusion leading to obvious mistakes by the market. One example is in the municipal bond market. There was an incident from our youth where we were really young.
turns.zh: 在因名称混淆而让市场犯下明显错误这方面，历史可不少。有一个例子是在市政债（municipal bond）市场。有一桩事发生在我们年轻时、我们都很小的时候。

turns.en: An Orange County, California, where they did all these derivatives trades and the municipal stuff lasted the municipal bonds of Orange County, Florida, Orange County, New York.
turns.zh: 加州有个橙县（Orange County, California），他们做了大量衍生品交易爆雷，而它拖累的是市政债——橙县，然后佛罗里达州橙县、纽约州橙县——

turns.en: I think there's an Orange County Indiana. They all got smoked. Why doesn't it really make a lesson? OK, but there are way more extreme versions of that, of which one of my favorites is we had a grad student who wrote a fantastic paper called Massively Confused Investors Making Conspicuously Ignorant Choices Parentheses MCI-MCIC.
turns.zh: 我想还有印第安纳州橙县。它们全被砸得很惨。这其实算不上什么有用的教训，好吧。但还有比这更极端的版本，我最喜欢的一个案例是：我们有个研究生写了一篇绝妙的论文，叫《大规模混淆的投资者做出显著无知的选择》，括号缩写 MCI、MCIC。

turns.en: That was the one I was thinking of. Yeah. Yeah. So MCI, the Microwave Communications Corporation, which had huge problems. They had the ticker MCIC, I guess, because they were a NASDAQ.
turns.zh: 哦，我刚才想的正是这个。对。所以 MCI（Microwave Communications Corporation）当时有一堆麻烦事。他们持有 MCIC 这个代码，我想是因为他们在纳斯达克（NASDAQ）。

turns.en: Let's see where and the company that had the ticker MCI, which was a completely unrelated company, would get destroyed every time. I think there was a closed end fund or something.
turns.zh: 让我想想，而另一个持有 MCI 代码的公司，是一家完全不相关的公司，可每次 MCI 出事它就被砸得很惨。我想那是一家封闭式基金（closed-end fund）之类的东西。

turns.en: MCI, maybe something like that. The last story on this is about a closed end fund. And this is maybe now, gosh, it's probably 10 years ago, time flies.
turns.zh: 哦对，MCI，大概是那样的。最后一个故事就是关于一家封闭式基金的。这可能是——天哪——大概 10 年前了，时间过得真快。

turns.en: When Barack Obama was president and he opened relations with Cuba, the closed end fund with the ticker CUBA Cuba went up, I think, over 100 percent and stayed up for weeks, maybe months.
turns.zh: 巴拉克·奥巴马（Barack Obama）当总统、他开启与古巴（Cuba）关系正常化的时候，那家代码是 CUBA 的封闭式基金——它跟古巴毫无关系——涨了上去，我想涨了超过 100%，而且持续了好几个星期，甚至好几个月。

turns.en: And that ticker had nothing to do with Cuba. That fund had nothing to do with Cuba. But it's just that because the ticker spelled out CUBA, it rocketed up.
turns.zh: 而那个代码虽然拼出来是 CUBA，但那家基金跟古巴一点关系都没有。就因为代码拼出来是 CUBA，它就一飞冲天。

turns.en: And if you could get borrow on it, that was a real money maker. But of course, there was the risk that it was going to triple in your face before it came back down.
turns.zh: 如果你能借到券做空它，那可是个真正的赚钱机器。但当然，也存在风险：它可能在你面前先翻三倍，之后才回落。

turns.en: So these things are not as easy to take advantage of as you might like. All right. So we talked about factors and puzzles. And so here's where I'd love to finish the conversation.
turns.zh: 所以这些机会并不像你以为的那样容易利用。好。——那么，我们聊了因子和谜题。这正是我想为这段对话收尾的地方。

turns.en: I want to spend some time on what you're doing on the private equity kind of replication side of things. I'll start with Cliff Asnes had done some work on Warren Buffett's performance.
turns.zh: 我想花点时间谈谈你在私募股权复制（PE replication）这方面正在做的事。我先从 Cliff Asness 说起，他对 Warren Buffett 的业绩做过一些研究。

turns.en: And he essentially was able to triangulate and really illustrate to a large extent that Buffett was a value manager and that, you know, a lot of his excess returns were linked to the value factor, I think, maybe quality was in there as well.
turns.zh: 他基本上能够三角定位、在很大程度上表明 Buffett 是一位价值（value）风格管理人，他的很多超额收益都与价值因子挂钩，我想可能也有质量（quality）在里面。

turns.en: So another friend of ours, a colleague of yours at Harvard, Eric Stafford, I studied with when you were the TA at Ferfama. He's done some seminal work on PE replication through factors.
turns.zh: 那么我们的另一位朋友、你在哈佛的一位同事 Eric Stafford——我在你当 Fama 助教那会儿也跟他同学过——他就用因子做私募股权复制，做了些开创性的工作。

turns.en: Take us through just how you are thinking about that, what he did and how you and your business partners are running with that. By the way, you can see how we're right back to our theme from earlier on my hypothetical manager who makes the small cap that right.
turns.zh: 给我们讲讲你目前是怎么思考这件事的、他做了什么，以及你和你的商业伙伴们怎么把它做起来。顺便，你可以看到我们又回到了前面那个主题——就是我那个做小盘股的假设管理人，对吧？

turns.en: Buffett with his value and quality bets. Do we say this guy's a genius who came up with these ideas of value and quality? Do we say, oh, gosh, well, you could just buy value and quality stocks and do as well as Buffett.
turns.zh: Buffett 带着他的价值和质量押注。我们到底说这人是位想出价值和质量这些点子的天才呢？还是说，哦，你完全可以去买价值股和质量股，就能做得和 Buffett 一样好。

turns.en: I think in Buffett's case, he deserves a lot of credit because this was not stuff that everybody else was doing. The whole idea of quality investing, probably he should be viewed as the father of value investing.
turns.zh: 我觉得就 Buffett 而言，他理应得到很多赞誉，因为这些并不是当时其他人都在做的事。整个“质量投资”的理念，他大概应该被视为价值投资之父。

turns.en: Obviously, he gives credit to people even before him. But these are not the answers are not obvious to those questions. But yeah, so I started thinking about alongside many years ago, I gave a speech here at HBS in 2000, in which I asked the question, boy, what if you just isn't leveraged buyout?
turns.zh: 显然，他把功劳给了更早的人。但对这些问题，答案并不显而易见。不过，是的，我早在多年前就开始思考这件事了。我在 2000 年在这里的 HBS 做过一次演讲，我在演讲里提出了一个问题：假如，不就是杠杆收购（leveraged buyout，LBO）吗？

turns.en: I talk about liquid private equity. I should really probably say liquid LBO, you know, liquid venture is an interesting idea. Liquid real estate, these are good ideas too, but they're a little different.
turns.zh: 我谈的是液态私募股权（liquid private equity）。我或许其实应该说液态 LBO。液态风险投资（liquid venture）是个有意思的想法。液态房地产也是好想法，但它们稍微不太一样。

turns.en: But so if we just say, so just for purposes of conversation, if I say liquid PE, I mean LBO. If you think about what LBO deal is, they're going to try to find a company that is, and in fact, it's exactly the things you said, quality and value.
turns.zh: 那就这样吧，就为了我们这场对话，如果我说“液态 PE”，我指的就是 LBO。你想想一笔 LBO 交易是什么，他们会去找一家公司——事实上恰恰就是你刚才说的那些特质：质量和价值。

turns.en: Let's just think about it for a second. What's an LBO deal? Well, you're going to buy a company, almost always a private company. And you're, you know, 90 some percent of deals are private to private.
turns.zh: 我们稍微想一下。一笔 LBO 交易是什么？你要买下一家公司，几乎总是私人公司，而且大约九成以上的交易是私人对私人（private to private）。

turns.en: You're going to buy it with maybe two thirds debt. It used to be more like three quarters. Now it's close to two thirds because interest rates are up.
turns.zh: 你会用大概三分之二的债务来买它。以前大概是四分之三，现在接近三分之二，因为利率上来了。

turns.en: You're going to pay something. You're going to pay on that debt something like nine to 12 percent. Use could be more like seven or eight, but you know, interest rates are up.
turns.zh: 你要为这部分债务付利息，大概 9% 到 12%。以前大概是 7% 或 8%，但你也知道，利率上来了。

turns.en: If you pay nine to 12 percent on two thirds of the value of the company, that is six to eight percent of enterprise value that you are paying out in interest every year.
turns.zh: 如果你为公司价值的三分之二付 9% 到 12% 的利息，那就相当于你每年要拿出企业价值（enterprise value）的 6% 到 8% 来付利息。

turns.en: Okay. So now what kinds of companies is that going to be possible to do? Well, first of all, it better be highly profitable. If the company doesn't make a lot of money, how are you going to pay out six, seven, eight percent of enterprise value in cash every year in interest?
turns.zh: 好。那么什么样的公司能办得到呢？首先，它最好盈利性很强。如果一家公司赚不了多少钱，你怎么可能每年拿出企业价值的 6%、7%、8% 的现金来付利息？

turns.en: It's going to have to be profitable, but you're going to need a low multiple too. Because if you buy it for 30 times earnings, one over 30 is 3.3 percent, not six to eight percent.
turns.zh: 它得是有盈利的，但你还需要一个低的估值倍数（multiple）。因为如果你用 30 倍盈利来买它，1 除以 30 只有 3.3%，而不是 6% 到 8%。

turns.en: Right. So you put that together and you say, okay, these are going to be high profit, low multiple firms. We might call that quality and value.
turns.zh: 对。所以你把这两点合起来，你就会说：好，这些将是高盈利、低倍数的公司。我们或许可以把它叫作“质量”和“价值”。

turns.en: By the way, we can push further on this. They're going to need to have a high payout ratio. If you have an Amazon type company that makes tons of money, but plows every penny back into gross for towards world conquest, that may be a wonderful company to buy.
turns.zh: 顺便说，我们可以再往下推一层。它们还需要有高的派息比例（payout ratio）。如果你有一家像 Amazon 那样的公司，赚很多钱，但把每一分钱都重新投回去、朝着征服世界去，那可能是一家很棒的要买的公司。

turns.en: But you don't want to LBO it because you're going to take the gross money and use it to pay interest and then that kills your growth plan. Right.
turns.zh: 但你不想去 LBO 它，因为你要拿走那些本可以用来付利息的钱，这会毁掉你的增长计划。对吧。

turns.en: So you need high profit and high payout. And then on the low side, you need low multiple. You also need low risk. Nobody's going to lend you two thirds of the value of the company and their moderate interest rate if the risk is crazy high.
turns.zh: 所以你需要高盈利和高派息。而在低的那一面，你需要低倍数，你还需要低风险。如果风险高得离谱，没人会用适中的利率借给你相当于公司价值三分之二的那笔钱。

turns.en: Right. But then also these are private companies. So they are going to, there's only a handful of private companies in the whole country that would be considered large cap if they were a public.
turns.zh: 对。但另外，这些都是私人公司。所以整个国家里，只有为数不多的几家私人公司，如果它们是上市公司的话会被算作大盘股。

turns.en: So these are going to look like small and mid cap companies or smaller. So high profit, high payout, low multiple, low risk, small size. These are the five things that make you what I call an LBO of old company.
turns.zh: 所以这些看起来会是中小盘、或者更小的公司。所以高盈利、高派息、低倍数、低风险、小规模——这五件事，就构成了我所说的“LBO 目标公司”。

turns.en: But as I know, you've noticed, because we studied together, the five pharma French factors, the exact five things that Jean can identify as the things that lead to outperformance in the public markets are the five things that you have to do as an LBO manager.
turns.zh: 而据你所知，你注意到了，因为我们一起同过学——Fama-French 的五个因子，Gene 能识别出的、在公开市场带来超额收益的那五个要素，恰恰就是你作为 LBO 管理人必须做的五件事。

turns.en: Right. It's kind of cool, actually, because we can imagine some curmudgeonly leveraged by out person real old school Wall Street guy hates academia, hates quant, hates Jean, hates me, hates the Nobel Prize.
turns.zh: 对吧。这其实挺妙的，因为我们能设想某个脾气古怪的杠杆收购老手——一个非常老派的华尔街家伙——他讨厌学术、讨厌量化、讨厌 Gene、讨厌我、讨厌诺贝尔奖。

turns.en: He still bets the right way on all five factors because it is baked into the model. And now we can see why he does so well, because first of all, they are really good at identifying the areas of the economy that are thriving because they own companies in every area of the economy.
turns.zh: 他照样在五个因子上都押对了方向，因为这已经烘焙进了这个模式里。于是我们现在能明白他为什么做得这么好，因为首先，他们真的很擅长识别经济里蓬勃发展的领域，因为他们在经济的各个领域都拥有公司。

turns.en: And there's some good research on this old research by Mark Critsman, who was my colleague at MIT. And over time, different elements of the economic story of play out.
turns.zh: 关于这点有一些不错的研究，是 Mark Critzman 做的一个老研究，他曾是我在 MIT 的同事。随着时间推移，经济叙事里的不同元素会轮流上演。

turns.en: We've gotten smarter. You know, Mark did just the most basic thing you could do in terms of industry tilts, you can do it better now, but you take the wisdom that these people legitimately have because they are very talented, hardworking people.
turns.zh: 我们变得更聪明了。你知道，Mark 当年在行业暴露（industry tilts）上做的只是你能做的最基本的事，你现在可以做得更好。但你采纳的是这些人确确实实拥有的智慧，因为他们是非常有才华、非常努力的人。

turns.en: And they're finding the right areas of the economy to bet on. And then the companies are thinking within those areas are the ones that bet the right way on all five farmer French factors.
turns.zh: 他们在找到经济里值得下注的正确领域。然后在这些领域里挑中的公司，正是那五件事都押对了 Fama-French 五个因子的公司。

turns.en: Of course, they're in the private markets. But boy, it seems like if you did this in the public markets, it ought to work. And then on top of that, and of course, Eric wrote this wonderful paper where he said, look, let's start by buying mid cap value or whatever version of these, you know, whether you saw five of the factors or some of them.
turns.zh: 当然，它们是在私人市场里。但天哪，看起来如果你在公开市场里也这么做，它应该管用。然后在此之上，当然，Eric 写了那篇精彩的论文，他说：好，我们从一个买入中盘价值股——或者这些因子的某个版本——不管是五个因子都占、还是只占其中一些——

turns.en: Let's start from that. Now let's lever it up a little bit because these folks are levered. Now, there's a debate as to how much leverage is really implicit in LBO.
turns.zh: 我们先从这里出发。现在我们把它稍微加一点杠杆，因为这些人本身就是加了杠杆的。至于 LBO 里隐含的杠杆到底有多少，一直有争论。

turns.en: You'll see people who say it's two to one or more. You'll see other people who say, oh, they're not really any more levered than the market.
turns.zh: 你会看到有人说大概是两倍或更多。你也会看到其他人说，哦，他们的杠杆其实并不比市场更高。

turns.en: My view is this typical public company is only 30% debt. These are not typical. These are the LBO public companies. They might be more like 40, 50% debt.
turns.zh: 我的看法是：一家典型的上市公司只有 30% 的债务。而这些不是典型公司，这些是 LBO 公司。它们的债务可能有 40%、50%。

turns.en: Typical LBO deal these days, maybe 60, 70% debt. So you're talking about 0.3 or 0.4 turns of leverage. And I can say that the first time I gave this talk, Don Rain and the chief strategist at Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, CPPIB, was in the audience and he came up and said, we've done the analysis in the right amount for the leverages, 0.3 or 0.4.
turns.zh: 如今一笔典型的 LBO 交易，可能有 60%、70% 的债务。所以你说的其实是 0.3 或 0.4 倍的额外杠杆。我还记得第一次讲这个演讲时，Don——加拿大养老金计划投资委员会（CPPIB）的首席策略师——他在听众席，走过来跟我说：我们做过分析，正确的杠杆幅度就是 0.3 或 0.4。

turns.en: And now it's 26 years later and I'm like, yeah, Don was right. I used to think it was higher, but I think Don's right. So point is you don't need to lever a ton.
turns.zh: 而 26 年过去了，我想：是啊，Don 是对的。我过去以为更高，但现在我觉得 Don 是对的。所以要点是，你不需要加太多杠杆。

turns.en: But even 0.3 or 0.4 is two or 3% a year of extra performance. And so now you say, all right, private equity does an amazing job. They pick the right areas of the economy.
turns.zh: 但哪怕只是 0.3 或 0.4 倍的杠杆，也能带来每年 2% 到 3% 的额外业绩。所以现在你会说：好，私募股权做得非常出色，他们挑对了经济里的领域。

turns.en: They pick the right companies within those areas. They lever up, you could do all those things in the public markets. And then the question is, if you do it, will you perform as well as PE?
turns.zh: 他们在这些领域里挑对了公司。他们加了杠杆——所有这些你都能在公开市场里做到。那么问题是：如果你这么做了，你能表现得像 PE 一样好吗？

turns.en: And the answer is, well, you won't in the sense that PE does other things that add value. They've got inside information on companies that as a public market investor, you will never be given.
turns.zh: 答案是：在某种意义上你不会那么出色，因为 PE 还做了其他创造价值的事。他们对公司有内幕信息，而作为公开市场投资者，你是永远拿不到的。

turns.en: And if you ever were, you wouldn't be allowed to trade that company anyway, be wrong and illegal. And they can make operational improvements to the companies, right?
turns.zh: 而且就算你拿到了，你也不会被允许去交易那家公司，那会是错误的、违法的。而且他们还能对公司做出运营上的改进，对吧？

turns.en: Now against that, they have to pay a control premium in order to get control to make those operational improvements. But I think that still leaves something for investors on the table.
turns.zh: 作为对立面，他们为了取得控制权、做出这些运营改进，必须支付控制权溢价（control premium）。但我认为这仍然给投资者留下了可观的价值。

turns.en: So they're outperforming, that is to say, traditional PE has edge from inside information, they have edge from the net of operational improvements minus the control premium.
turns.zh: 所以他们在跑赢——也就是说，传统 PE 靠内幕信息有优势，靠“运营改进净额减去控制权溢价”也有优势。

turns.en: And then there is the smoothing. And Cliff, of course, has been, I think the person who's spoken the most eloquently on this. Oxford has done incredible research on this.
turns.zh: 然后还有平滑化（smoothing）。当然，Cliff 一直是——我认为——在这点上讲得最有说服力的人。牛津在这方面做了了不起的研究。

turns.en: And Cliff has a way with words and he says, look, the way that when the market crashes and it's down 20% and we know the PE LBO is levered more than the market, so they ought to be down between 25 and 30%.
turns.zh: Cliff 很会遣词造句，他说：你看，当市场崩盘、跌 20% 时——我们知道 PE 的 LBO 杠杆比市场更高，所以它们本该跌 25% 到 30%。

turns.en: And then they'll announce, oh, COVID hit, but we're only down 10%. Cliff called it volatility laundry. And that is a really witty phrase. If you want to do the equivalent of what PE does in the public markets, people are going to expect you to deliver that smooth performance profile.
turns.zh: 然后他们会宣布：哦，新冠疫情来了，但我们只跌了 10%。Cliff 把它叫做“波动率洗衣”（volatility laundry）。这真是个妙语。如果你想用公开市场里等价的做法来复刻 PE 做的事，人们会期待你交付那种平滑的业绩曲线。

turns.en: If the market crashes 20 and PE says they're down 10 and you have some kind of liquid private equity and you're down 25 to 30, people will be enraged.
turns.zh: 如果市场崩了 20，而 PE 说他们只跌 10，而你有某种液态私募股权却跌了 25 到 30，人们会怒不可遏。

turns.en: They'll say, you're just levered market, you're not liquid PE. So you need to overlay a hedge to satisfy investors who have that concern. And that's not every investor, but the investors who are worried about that smoothness, you need to overlay a hedge and there may be costs associated with that.
turns.zh: 他们会说：你只是一个加了杠杆的市场而已，你不是液态 PE。所以你需要针对那些在意这种关切的投资者，叠加一个对冲，让业绩平滑。虽然不是每个投资者都在意，但那些担心平滑性的投资者，你需要叠加一个对冲，而这可能带来一些成本。

turns.en: And then you say, well, wait a minute, Randy, you're saying you're going to deliver PE like performance. And I would tell you that my view is if you look, since I gave that speech, I think it really has worked.
turns.zh: 然后你会说：等等，Randy，你是说你能交付 PE 般的业绩。而我会告诉你，我的看法是：自从我做那个演讲以来，这种思路实际上真的管用了。

turns.en: This approach really has worked to deliver PE like performance. But wait a minute, you're behind because you're going to have to pay up for those derivatives and even with superstar derivative people on your side advising you, like Dean Kerner, that's going to probably not make money.
turns.zh: 这种方式确实管用，能交付 PE 般的业绩。但等等，你还是落后的，因为你得花大价钱买那些衍生品，而且就算有你那边超级明星的衍生品高手给你出主意——像 Dean Kernott——这可能也赚不到钱。

turns.en: Buying insurance is not generally a money maker. And then you're not going to get the inside information they get. And then you've got this loss from operational improvements minus control premium, you're really behind PE.
turns.zh: 买保险通常不是一件赚钱的事。而且你拿不到他们那种内幕信息。然后你还得承担“运营改进减去控制权溢价”这一块损失，你真的落后于 PE。

turns.en: And the answer is absolutely liquid PE on a gross basis is going to be three to 6% a year, I would claim, behind traditional PE. But once you add up operator fees, monetary fees, origination fees, management fees, carrying interest, PE, according to a CalPERS study, charges over 700 basis points a year in fees.
turns.zh: 而答案是：绝对地，液态 PE 在毛收益（gross basis）上，我会说，会落后于传统 PE 每年 3% 到 6%。但一旦你把运营费、绩效费、募收费、管理费、附带权益（carried interest）都加起来——PE 根据一项 CalPERS 的研究，每年收取的费用超过 700 个基点。

turns.en: And so if you're running a liquid PE ETF or mutual fund or anything, but charging something like 100 dips, that is a really big gap, 700 to 100, 600 basis point gap, you could be three to 6% behind on a gross basis and still be even with PE or even ahead on a net basis.
turns.zh: 所以如果你运行一只液态 PE 的 ETF 或共同基金，或任何东西，但只收大概 100 个基点的费用，那就是一道非常大的鸿沟：700 对 100，600 个基点的差距。你可以在毛收益上落后 3% 到 6%，却仍然在净收益（net basis）上和 PE 打平、甚至领先。

turns.en: And so that's why I think the idea of liquid PE is so powerful. And you notice it doesn't have to compete with the notion is not, oh, my gosh, people should ditch their PE and put it in liquid PE.
turns.zh: 这就是为什么我觉得液态 PE 的理念如此强大。你注意到，它并不一定要竞争——想法不是“天哪，大家应该撤掉 PE，改投液态 PE”。

turns.en: The idea is for investors who can't invest in private equity because they're just not rich enough to make million dollar minimums. This is a solution to take their portfolio from 6040 to 50, 30, 20.
turns.zh: 它的定位是：对于投不起私募股权、还没富有到能满足一百万美元起投门槛的人，这是一个解决方案，把他们的组合从 60/40 调整到 50、30、20。

turns.en: And for institutional investors and wealthy families who are PE investors, this can play a really useful role as a tool of the toolbox for them as a liquidity buffer for completion portfolios, for other kinds of applications that are hard to do with traditional PE.
turns.zh: 而对于那些本身就是 PE 投资者的机构投资者和富裕家族，它可以作为工具箱里的一个工具发挥非常实用的作用——充当流动性缓冲、用于完成性组合，以及很多用传统 PE 难以实现的其他用途。

turns.en: Yeah, I would say the vol laundering is a great turn of phrase. But we'll also say it's become a feature, not a bug, but it is a bug. It's hard to look at that and think that you're really getting something for free as a derivatives focused investor.
turns.zh: 是啊，我会说“波动率洗衣”是个很妙的说法。但我们也会说，它已经成了一种“功能”、而不是“缺陷”——可它确实是个缺陷。作为一个专注衍生品的投资者，很难看着那个然后认为你真的在白白得到什么好处。

turns.en: You really got to focus on mark to market risk. So that's very near and dear to me. I want to walk through the portfolio construction process.
turns.zh: 你真的必须盯住盯市（mark to market）风险。所以那一点对我特别切身。我想走一遍这个组合构建的过程。

turns.en: So we've got these five factors. You also have essentially a database of PE returns. So you're trying, you're solving for a return stream. And not just returns, but holdings, right?
turns.zh: 那么我们有这五个因子。你同时还基本上拥有私募股权收益的一个数据库。所以你在求解一条收益流——而且不只是收益，还有持仓，对吧？

turns.en: A crucial element here is if you're going to buy what PE buys, you got to know what they've got and that data is not generally available. There is certain kinds of data you can buy in the market.
turns.zh: 这里一个关键的要素是：如果你要买 PE 买的东西，你就得知道他们持有什么，而那些数据通常是拿不到的。市场上你能买到某些种类的数据。

turns.en: It's very expensive and it gives you a limited peak into what PE is holding. But if you really want to know what PE is holding, you have to partner with one of the handful of firms in the world that actually have the data on everything going on in PE.
turns.zh: 它非常贵，而且只给你一个有限的、窥探 PE 持仓的窗口。但如果你真的想知道 PE 持有什么，你必须与世界上少数几家真正拥有 PE 全部动态数据的其中一家公司合作。

turns.en: And if you do that, then you can get access to the deep insights on what PE is doing now and what they're doing next quarter and what they did 20 years ago so that you can do the analysis and so forth.
turns.zh: 如果你那样做，你就能获得对 PE 现在在做什么、下季度在做什么、以及 20 年前做过什么的深刻洞察，从而你可以做分析等等。

turns.en: Well, you mentioned SpaceX before, I assume SpaceX is not going to show up in a PE screen. So these are old economy, perhaps stodgy industries, maybe not as sexy as some of the high flying stuff, as you said.
turns.zh: 嗯，你之前提到过 SpaceX，我猜 SpaceX 不会出现在一个 PE 筛选结果里。所以这些是老经济、也许有点沉闷的行业，可能不像某些高飞的东西那样性感，正如你所说。

turns.en: Although he's very heavy in software and services these days and has been one of the reason they've been so successful is they were early to see that software had pivoted from a world of a lot of APRWARE to being something that chunked out profits regularly.
turns.zh: 不过现在 PE 在软件和服务上其实非常重，而且它们一直这么成功的原因之一，就是它们很早就看出软件已经从过去那种形态，转变成能定期产出利润的东西。

turns.en: And of course, now we had the SAS Pocalypse and now I hear we're having the SAS Assance and no one's quite sure where it's headed. Is everybody going to be home coding all their business software or is business software going to be bigger than ever?
turns.zh: 当然，现在我们经历了 SaaS-pocalypse（软件即服务末日论），现在我又听说我们在经历 SaaS-ascendance，没人真正清楚它往哪走。是不是大家都会回家自己写所有的商业软件？还是说商业软件会比以往更大？

turns.en: And PE is making bets in that area and we're closely watching to see what they're doing so that we can make similar bets in the public markets because that's how you do it.
turns.zh: PE 正在那个领域下注，而我们正密切观察他们在做什么，好让我们在公开市场里也能做类似的押注，因为就是这么干的。

turns.en: You really got to stay up to date and these folks are better situated than anybody to do the deep research and see where the opportunities are.
turns.zh: 你真的得紧跟前沿，而这些人比任何人都更有条件去做深度研究、看清机会在哪里。

turns.en: Take us through the process of seeing what is owned and then also overlaying these factors as a way of, I don't want to say predicting what they'll own, but I assume these factors play some role in accounting for the returns.
turns.zh: 带我们走一遍这个过程——先看清他们持有什么，然后再把这些因子叠加进去，作为一种方式——我不想说是预测他们会持有什么，但我猜这些因子在解释收益上起一定作用。

turns.en: Absolutely right. In other words, first, you're trying to figure out the kinds of companies they're buying. You want to find similar companies in the public markets in terms of what they're doing, right?
turns.zh: 完全正确。换句话说，首先你要弄清他们正在买的公司是哪一类。你要在公开市场里找到在经营上相似的公司，对吧？

turns.en: Say, here are the areas in the economy where there is huge demand and things are growing fast and all that. So then you need to identify the public companies that match on that dimension and there will be less.
turns.zh: 比如说：这些是经济里需求巨大、增长飞快的领域。然后你需要找出在那个维度上相匹配的公开公司，而符合条件的会少一些。

turns.en: And then from those, you need to take the subset that say, Hey, this one, yeah, it's a nice match, except it's trading at 40 times earnings.
turns.zh: 然后从那些里面，你需要挑出这样一个子集，即：嘿，这个匹配得不错，只不过它的估值是 40 倍盈利。

turns.en: That's not a fit for what we're trying to accomplish here. The market caught on to this one. You got to find the one that's not a 40 times earnings yet and you got to find the one that's already profitable and not the one that looks similar, but they're not making money yet and so forth.
turns.zh: 那就不符合我们要达成的目标。市场已经看上了这一只。你得找到那个还没到 40 倍盈利的，你得找到那个已经盈利的，而不是那个看起来类似、但还没赚钱的公司，如此等等。

turns.en: So you really need to match on those characteristics at the same time. And then once you've identified a portfolio of say 200 companies and notice the LBO portfolio, if you, you know, there's like a thousand LBO funds in America, they have about 10,000 positions.
turns.zh: 所以你真的得同时在这些特征上做匹配。然后一旦你识别出一个大概 200 家公司的组合——你注意，LBO 那一边，大概美国有一千家 LBO 基金，它们合起来有大约一万个持仓。

turns.en: If you add up the entire universe of LBO deals, we were looking in liquid PE to find the 200 public companies that are maximally similar portfolio wise to the portfolio of 10,000 private companies.
turns.zh: 如果把整个 LBO 交易的宇宙加起来——我们做液态 PE 时，是要在一万个私人公司的组合里，找出 200 家在组合层面最为相似的公开公司。

turns.en: And then you say, Hey, boosted a little bit with leverage. So, you know, if you have a billion in the farm, you might buy 1.3 billion worth of those stocks, then overlay some well thought out hedges.
turns.zh: 然后你说：好，再用杠杆稍微放大一点。比如你如果有一亿美元的资金，你可能会买入 1.3 亿美元的这些股票，然后再叠加一些深思熟虑的对冲。

turns.en: It might be something as simple as buying put spreads, you know, 95, 85 foot spread, but more likely you want to be a lot smarter than that.
turns.zh: 它可能简单到只是买入看跌期权价差（put spread），比如 95、85 的看跌价差，但更可能你需要比那聪明得多。

turns.en: And, you know, this is why I reach out to you to get in touch because, because I know you're a deep thinker on these derivatives subjects. And, you know, like, I know about derivatives in the sense that like, I'm a finance professor, it's my job to know something, but like derivatives are not for amateurs.
turns.zh: 你知道，这就是我为什么要主动联系你、跟你搭上线，因为我知道你在这些衍生品主题上是个深度思考者。就衍生品而言，我懂一点，因为我是一个金融教授，懂点是分内事，但衍生品可不是给外行玩的。

turns.en: And I am, let's say, high level amateur in derivatives. And we need to talk to real pros like you, if we're going to make smart decisions about the most efficient ways to get these hedges.
turns.zh: 我可以说自己在衍生品上是一个“高层次的外行”。而我们需要跟像你这样的真正高手交流，才能就获取这些对冲的最有效方式做出明智决策。

turns.en: And that's on two dimensions, right? A, the edge has to actually work, but also B, you can't spend a fortune on a hedge or you kill the golden goose.
turns.zh: 而且这是在两个维度上，对吧？A，对冲得真的管用；但 B，你也不能在对冲上花太多钱，否则你就把那只下金蛋的鹅（golden goose）给杀了。

turns.en: If you look at the kind of variation from the factor standpoint in terms of what the five factors will tell you that the portfolio ought to look like over time, you mentioned software, that's probably not something that would have come up a decade ago.
turns.zh: 如果你从因子角度看这种变化——就这五个因子会告诉你这个组合随时间该长什么样而言——你提到了软件，那大概是十年前不会浮现出来的东西。

turns.en: So the industries change, the characteristics change, and then the private equity portfolio changes. So I'd love for you to just talk to us a little bit about that.
turns.zh: 所以行业在变，特征在变，私募股权的组合也在变。所以我特别想让你跟我们多讲讲这方面。

turns.en: And then as another part of that is, as you're trying to replicate the returns, how close you've done a lot of regressions over the years, I'm sure.
turns.zh: 然后作为其中另一部分，在你试图复制收益的过程中——你这些年一定做过很多回归——

turns.en: How close do you think you're getting? How satisfied do you feel about the process? Yeah, you're absolutely right. Early 2000s, software was a huge underweight in P.
turns.zh: 你觉得你复制得有多接近？你对这个过程有多满意？——是啊，你说得完全对。在 2000 年代初，软件在 PE 里是一个巨大的低配。

turns.en: It was all sort of brownfields, industrials and things of that nature. And the businesses changed hugely over time. And in fact, it's funny because way back when we were in grad school together, I wrote a paper with my dear friend, Christopher Polk, called on the impact of industry factors and asset pricing test was like the worst title ever for a paper, we were closed grad students.
turns.zh: 那时候全是那种“棕地”（brownfields）工业之类。而 businesses 随时间发生了巨大的变化。其实很有意思，因为我们读研那会儿，我和我亲爱的朋友 Christopher Polk 合写过一篇论文，叫《论行业因子对资产定价检验的影响》——大概是史上最烂的论文标题之一，我们那会儿还是研究生。

turns.en: But the idea what we've shown the paper is, if you're going to buy a low multiple portfolio, value stock portfolio, the best way to do it is not to buy the hundred lowest multiple stocks.
turns.zh: 但那篇论文展示的是：如果你要买入一个低倍数的组合、一个价值股组合，最好的做法不是去买倍数最低的 100 只股票。

turns.en: It's to go to each sector of the economy and buy the lowest multiple stocks in that sector, because what you get is a much better diversified portfolio.
turns.zh: 而是走到经济的每个行业板块，买入那个板块里倍数最低的股票，因为你得到的是一个分散度好得多的组合。

turns.en: So you have way lower volatility of memory serves from the paper and from the 90s, there's lots of data since about two thirds of all by being diversified across industries of just buying all the lowest multiple companies, because you're just going to be like heavily weighted towards the out of favor sectors, if you do it that way.
turns.zh: 所以你的波动性会低得多——如果我没记错，那篇论文和 90 年代的数据（此后数据更多了）显示，大约三分之二相对于只买所有低倍数公司所降低的波动来自跨行业分散化，因为如果你只买低倍数公司，你会严重偏向那些不受待见的板块。

turns.en: And so you want to spread across this. And we found that the average return was actually a little bit higher, even though you were buying companies whose multiples weren't as low, nevertheless buying the low multiple software company and the low multiple biotech and the low multiple oil company and so on and so forth that worked better.
turns.zh: 所以你想把这些分散开来。我们发现平均收益实际上还略高一点，尽管你买的是一些倍数没那么低的公司——但买入低倍数的软件公司、低倍数的生物科技、低倍数的石油公司等等，反而更有效。

turns.en: This is the way you want to think about this is that you're identifying these characteristics, but you're also doing them in the parts of the economy that the PE is focused on.
turns.zh: 这就是你思考这件事的方式：你在识别这些特征，但你也把这些特征用在 PE 所聚焦的那些经济领域里。

turns.en: And so you're taking advantage of their wisdom on both those parts of it. And so that gives you a nicely diversified portfolio. And of course you have some of your bets even in the public markets, health care is bigger than banking, but in the last time I looked it was less than twice as big in PE and LDO, there's 15 times as much health care as there is banking these days, right?
turns.zh: 所以你在两方面都利用了他们的智慧。于是你得到一个分散得很好的组合。当然，在公开市场里，医疗保健（health care）的体量比银行大，但我上次看的时候它还不到银行的两倍大；而在 PE 和 LBO 里，如今的医疗保健是银行的 15 倍那么大，对吧？

turns.en: So you're going to have some real overweights and underweights. And as you say, they change all the time. And so you have to keep up and we'll be doing some trading.
turns.zh: 所以你会有一些真正的超配和低配。而且如你所说，它们一直在变。所以你得紧跟动态，我们也会做一些交易。

turns.en: And then of course you have the usual questions of is it worth trading weekly or monthly or quarterly or annually, how much you will pay in trading costs in order to get to the portfolio you like the best.
turns.zh: 然后当然，你还有那些老问题：值得每周、每月、每季还是每年交易一次？你愿意付多少交易成本，才能到达你最想要的那个组合？

turns.en: And so those are all hard portfolio management problems that we think about all the time. The other thing I just like about the concept is, look, the mag seven, the top of the S&P, you don't want to get in the way of that thing.
turns.zh: 所以这些都是很难的组合管理问题，我们无时无刻不在思考。这个概念让我喜欢的另一点是：你看，Magnificent 7（美股七巨头）、标普的头部，你不想挡在那样一个东西前面。

turns.en: That is just extraordinary. And you want something that's different, that just looks different and acts a little bit different. We've got to really force ourselves to think about diversification.
turns.zh: 那真是太过火了。你想要一些不同的、看起来不一样、走势也稍微不一样的东西。我们真的得强迫自己去思考分散化。

turns.en: It can't just be all those top seven to 10 stocks. And so this has just got a different equities or equities, but these are different sort of underlying businesses and different return drivers as well.
turns.zh: 不能全都是那前 7 到 10 只股票。所以这算是不同的股票——或者说也是股票，但它们是不同的底层企业，回报的驱动因素也不同。

turns.en: That's right. And look, it's a fascinating time with such a small number of companies all clustered in software slash high tech. And even Tesla probably would say most of the values in their software.
turns.zh: 没错。而且你看，这是一个迷人的时代——如此少的公司，全都挤在软件/高科技这一块。甚至 Tesla，我想他们大概也会说，自己的价值大部分在软件上。

turns.en: And it is really, and arguably even Nvidia, right, is really more about software than other things. I mean, I'm not claiming to be an Nvidia expert, but that's my sense.
turns.zh: 确实，甚至可以说 Nvidia 归根结底更是软件而非别的。我是说，我不敢自称是 Nvidia 专家，但这是我的感觉。

turns.en: When I talk to people and other stuff is that's been just a huge differentiator for them. It is incredible. If you look back just a short time, I think I did this three years ago and so I'll look back a decade.
turns.zh: 我跟别人聊下来，别的方面对他们来说一直是一个巨大的差异化因素，太惊人。如果往回看一小段时间——我想我三年前做过这个分析——那我把目光拉回十年。

turns.en: So I think it was 2013 that I was looking at and looked at the 10 biggest companies and first of all, the 10 biggest companies were like 17% of the market, not 30% or whatever they are.
turns.zh: 所以我想那是 2013 年，我当时在审视并查看了市值最大的 10 家公司，首先，最大的 10 家公司大概占市场的 17%，而不是现在 30% 或者随便多少。

turns.en: First of all, now, right. Last I looked like seven companies were like 30% of the market as opposed to 10 companies being like 17%. So it's double more than double the concentration, but also the 10 companies from 2013, you had JP Morgan Chase, you had Exxon Mobile, you had Johnson and Johnson, you had Microsoft.
turns.zh: 首先，现在——我上次看的时候，大概七家公司就占了市场 30%，而对比之下当年是十家公司占 17%。所以集中度是翻倍还不止。而且 2013 年那十家公司里有 JP Morgan Chase、有 Exxon Mobil、有 Johnson & Johnson、有 Microsoft。

turns.en: In other words, it was inconceivable that the economy could do well without that group of companies doing well, or that those companies could do well without meaning that there was good news for the economy.
turns.zh: 换句话说，那组公司不景气、经济却好，或者那组公司景气、经济上却没有好消息，都是不可想象的。

turns.en: And obviously markets can be predictors of the economy, not saying simultaneous, but in terms of, you know, it's just so different now where there's this cluster.
turns.zh: 显然市场可以是经济的先行指标——我并不是说它们同步——但就现在真的太不一样了，有这么一个集群。

turns.en: And I'm not here to tell you how much Tesla or how much Nvidia to buy. What I'm saying is that should be one part of your portfolio and then there should be another part of your portfolio.
turns.zh: 我不是来告诉你该买多少 Tesla 或多少 Nvidia。我要说的是，那应该是你组合的一部分，然后你的组合里还应该有另一部分。

turns.en: And this look would be, could be part of the portfolio. And sometimes we will say, well, how did this perform relative to the S&P? And it's kind of like, look, if everybody decides they hate Tesla this month and it's down a bunch, we look like geniuses compared to the S&P.
turns.zh: 而这类做法就可以是组合的一部分。有时候我们会说：这东西相对标普表现如何？这就有点像——如果这个月大家都决定讨厌 Tesla、它大跌，那我们跟标普一比就显得像天才。
